en: Volume Two, Part One.
Composed by Li Tongxuan of the Great Tang at Beiping. Chapter Ten:
Sudhana Entering the Stage and Accordance with Reality. From the first [section], "The City Walls of the Three Realms of Existence."
The first section consists of thirty-four lines of verse spoken by Sudhana, praising the suffering of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*) and the nature of all phenomena (*dharma*).

The second section, beginning from "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva turned like an elephant king," comprises both prose and verse; this is the portion in which Mañjuśrī praises Sudhana’s ability to resolve upon *bodhicitta* and exhorts him not to weary of the suffering of birth and death, thereby enabling him to fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra.

Third, from the point where Mañjuśrī has finished speaking the verses until his departure to travel southward, this section of prose sūtra constitutes the part in which Mañjuśrī praises Sudhana’s generation of the bodhicitta and reveals the category of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
The fourth [section] proceeds south toward the Land of Supreme Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*); this is the portion concerning Sudhana’s seeking of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
From here until the end of the sutra, including Mañjuśrī, there are fifty-three spiritual friends in total.

The fifty individuals clarify the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten stages, and the stage of equal enlightenment; each has ten spiritual friends as its primary positions, totaling fifty persons.

Taking these three—Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and Samantabhadra—as the great functioning of the principle and wisdom of the Buddha-fruit, they serve as the essence and function of the principle and wisdom within the cause and effect of the fifty dharma-gates of the five stages.

Within the fifty stages of advancement, this fundamental wisdom—the discerning, sublime prajñā of the signless Dharmakāya—is ever-present; within the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra, the myriad practices constitute both cause and effect.
Within each and every stage, these three factors are present, forming cause and effect.
There are fifty factors within the causes and fifty within the effects, totaling one hundred.
Regarding the five stages of the profound cause and effect, one constantly takes the ten pāramitās as the practice for ascending progress; this is termed "one hundred and ten.
These ten pāramitās always take fundamental wisdom, the formless Dharmakāya, and the myriad practices of Samantabhadra as their essence and function.

For example, when a practitioner has not yet resolved their mind [for enlightenment], the fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*) from beginningless time is severed all at once upon the initial resolution of the mind and the realization of the Path during the first stage (*bhūmi*). Thereafter, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) gradually diminish until they become faint; it is only then that the fruit of Buddhahood is finally attained through a gradual, step-by-step progression.
The subsequent fifty spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) have their own sequential order.

For instance, from the initial mind of the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi) up to the third abode on the summit of Mount Wondrous Peak, one is predominantly focused upon the true mind; this is represented by three bhikṣus.

From the third stage to the sixth stage, the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja, through his clear realization, turned back those conditions and focused primarily on the true mind; thus, he had to fully comprehend conventional phenomena.

By means of the elder Megha—who resided in the marketplace—and the elder Vimokṣaka—who practiced the gate of dhyāna—along with the single person of the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja, they collectively demonstrated that the turbid places of the world are themselves pure. Furthermore, they showed that the knowledge of letters, words, and phrases, as well as the myriad environments of the world, are all entirely liberation.

By means of these three individuals—two laypeople and one bhikṣu—the Dharma is manifested; this first clarifies the fulfillment of the six pāramitās, and subsequently clarifies supramundane and mundane liberation.

After these two kinds of liberation, by means of the seventh stage of expedient practice, one dwells perpetually within birth and death to nurture great kindness and great compassion; without wearying of birth and death, one keeps suffering sentient beings in mind while concurrently cultivating the work of wisdom.

Upon reaching the eighth stage, effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) is finally perfected within a single portion of pure worldly knowledge; this is then illustrated by the examples of the laywoman Pūrṇā and the seer Vimalakṣa, thereby clarifying the station of wisdom and compassion.
The seventh and eighth [stages] constitute the gate of perfecting the unity of wisdom and compassion, as these two states coexist at the place of the ocean tide.

The ninth [stage], by clarifying the purity of wisdom and fearlessness of the eight abodes, attains the divine power of immortality; it is able to act in concert with those of wrong views and other heterodox paths, leading those who follow such deviant currents back to right view.

The practice of "scorching the body with five fires," where flames reach the heavens, and the boundless "mountain of knives," such as climbing the mountain of knives and entering the mass of fire, are represented by the Brahmin Śreyas.

The tenth [chapter] brings together the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as the consummation of the practice of wisdom and compassion; this is illustrated by the compassionate conduct of the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja.
King Siṃhadhvaja represents wisdom, while the daughter represents compassion, serving as the illustration.

The seventh is the Upāsikā Pūrṇā; in Sanskrit, she is called Śūradattā. Beginning with the practice of skillful means, she entered into birth and death to nurture her great compassion; because she still retained residual habitual tendencies, she was represented by the title of an Upāsikā.
Upon reaching the tenth dwelling (*vihāra*), one clarifies how compassion proceeds from wisdom without being stained by habitual tendencies; this is symbolized by the maiden Siṃhadhvaja-rāja-kanyā.

Because the wisdom and compassion produced through the cultivation of the five stages differ in their maturity, it is necessary to engage with the essence and function of the principle and wisdom of the single-vehicle (*ekayāna*) Buddha-fruition. Through the successive and alternating engagement with the ten dwellings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one undergoes refinement through the fifty perfections (*pāramitā*). Only then does one attain the various arts of wisdom and compassion, at which point all matters are finalized and merit is perfected.

If one were to seek merely the principle of liberation that transcends the world, there would be no single dharma at all; such a person would be identical to the limited path of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Two Vehicles and could not be called a Teacher of Gods and Humans.

If one seeks the unsurpassed Buddha-vehicle, the vehicle of omniscience, one must remain within birth and death without emerging or sinking; one must clearly understand great wisdom, great compassion, and all arts and skills, for it cannot be that one who lacks wisdom and knowledge is a Buddha.
The Sūtra states: "The Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, for he has thoroughly realized all dharmas.
This clarifies that the Buddha's Dharma-body is characterized by there being nothing he does not know and nothing he does not understand.

Thus, these five stages and fifty gates of practice, comprising one hundred and ten layers of cause and effect, all take the fundamental wisdom of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra as their essence and function. Therefore, through Mañjuśrī’s wondrous wisdom, one skillfully discriminates all phenomena; through Samantabhadra’s wisdom of differentiation, one clearly knows the capacities of all sentient beings and acts in accordance with them. This fundamental wisdom is designated as the Buddha: it is eternally without fabrication, its own nature is like space, it does not belong to the three periods of time, and it lacks the nature of past, present, or beginning and end, being identical to the immeasurable eons of the world.

However, wisdom has no temporal sequence; it is without distinction between beginning and end, without transition from practice to fruit, and remains undefiled while dwelling in the world, taking fundamental wisdom as the essence of all practices.

For this Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle, fundamental wisdom is taken as the fruit of Buddhahood; clear wisdom is taken as the initial arousal of the bodhicitta; and the attainment of Buddhahood in a single lifetime is taken as the fruit of practice within these five stages, for it is the method of teaching and practice common to this [vehicle].

By being in accord with fundamental wisdom, there is no arising throughout past, present, or future kalpas, whether few or many; therefore, one perceives that the original nature of all sentient beings is non-arising, which is, in sum, the single birth.

Now, upon seeing the Way, one attains Buddhahood simultaneously with all Buddhas of the past and future; this is just as within Maitreya’s pavilion, where the kalpas of the three periods of time are manifested as being entirely present in the current moment, for such is the nature of the Dharma within the realm of wisdom.
To cause those who have resolved their minds to realize that this activity of wisdom is likewise so, one does not perceive many lifetimes; this is called the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
Within the realm of wisdom, there is no measure of temporal divisions such as the three periods of past, present, and future, for such is the fundamental nature of phenomena.

To see even a small amount of delusion is itself delusion; it is the karma of consciousness, it is birth and death, it is the obstacle of clinging, and it is false view. One must follow what is correct and not follow what is false.
Therefore, these fifty spiritual friends constitute the practice for ascending progress.

Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya represent the cause and effect of the essence and function of principle and wisdom within these fifty stages; from beginning to end, they do not depart from these dharmas of the three periods of time.
This constitutes one hundred and ten dharma-gates, as previously described.

The preceding four sections have already clarified the exhortation and praise for Sudhana’s ability to resolve upon bodhicitta, as well as the formal indication of the locations of the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
The following clarifies Sudhana’s departure, his pursuit of entry into the correct [path] and the bodhisattva practices.
This subsequent section, beginning from here, clarifies the entry into the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*).
Within the first gate among the ten stages of abiding (*bhūmi*), the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is primary, with the other nine serving as its companions.

To the south there is a land named "Supreme Joy" (*Vaijayanta*). "South" signifies correctness, illumination, and the sun; it represents emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and literary expression. It is the mind that transcends phenomena; through the illuminating mind one penetrates emptiness, whereby wisdom and literary expression become naturally clear, and correct wisdom manifests before one.

Therefore, when paying homage to the Buddha, one first utters "Namo. This takes the East as the beginning because the East is the source of spring's growth and manifestation; as it is the head of all things that arise, it serves as the commencement of all Dharma rites.
The south is designated as the primary gateway to the Dharma and as the foremost of emptiness and true wisdom; therefore, it is mentioned first.
The east is considered the vanguard for the emergence and manifestation of all things; therefore, it is established as the foremost of all Dharma activities.
Therefore, the character for "East" (東) is formed by a wooden pin piercing the sun, because wood generates brightness.
By means of the character for "Wood," one governs the dharmas of the ten directions; likewise, the character for "South" (南) also governs the dharmas of the ten directions.

Taking the eighth of the ten lower signs as the character for wood, taking the eastern direction as the Azure Dragon and as wisdom, and representing this by the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra residing in the east;

taking Avalokiteśvara as compassion, representing his station in the west—where west is metal, the White Tiger, and slaughter—to represent the Dharma of compassion acting within the realms of slaughter and evil destinies.
Therefore, within the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the two gates of wisdom and compassion are harmonized.
Avalokiteśvara was on the western slope of Mount Vajra, where he beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva arriving from the east; thus they met together.
Amitābha represents wisdom and Avalokiteśvara represents compassion; both take on directional forms because they manifest these qualities through symbols.
Yet, one direction inherently encompasses all ten directions.
For now, I shall briefly describe a small portion of the meaning of the character for "East" (木) to clarify that the symbolic dharma cannot be fully expressed in words.

The character for "wood" symbolizes the perfection of wisdom pervading the ten directions; it extends horizontally and penetrates vertically, encompassing the methods of the Eight Trigrams within its entirety. It incorporates the methods of both the upper and lower directions, thereby constituting the perfection of wisdom pervading the ten directions. If even a single method were lacking, it could not be called perfect wisdom.
Furthermore, for example, the east corresponds to the trigram Zhen; Zhen represents wood, the eldest son, sound, and command, which thus pervades and penetrates all ten directions.
Furthermore, for instance, sounds and speech issue from the mouth; thus, the mouth is *Dui*.
*Xun* represents verbal expression and the teaching of the wind; *Li* represents literary composition, the mind, the eyes, and the void.
Qian represents the circular and pure.
Kun represents the multitude of those who are faithful and compliant, and it represents the belly.
Kan represents water, the Dark Warrior (Xuanwu), and deceitful wickedness; these are what the wise govern.
Gen represents the mountain, the young boy, the ignorant child, and cessation.
Above is Heaven, which contains and encompasses all phenomena.
Therefore, within the stage of the Ten Faiths, the world above is named Equality; the Buddha’s title is Observing Wisdom, signifying that fundamental wisdom takes empty space as its essence.

Below, in the directions of Wu and Ji, earth reigns during the four seasons; this symbolizes the perfection of wisdom and compassion, bearing all things, and through the dharma of one direction, pervading the ten directions.
If the myriad images throughout the ten directions are used to encompass the various categories of beings within the world,

and if the Way of the Gentleman is made luminous such that the principles of the ten directions are constantly present within the perpetual application of a single mind, only then can it serve as right wisdom, as illumination, as the sun, and as elegant literature.
Therefore, the eight thousand characters of the ten gates constitute the character "Nan" (南), signifying that the south represents correctness and clarity.
On the day the sun reaches the eighth degree, one uses an eight-foot gnomon in the southern direction to determine the expansion and contraction of its shadow.
This is a brief summary;
the full details are as follows.

As for what is here called the "Southern [Tradition]," it is so designated because ten kinds of wisdom are there perpetually perfected, thereby enabling one to definitively distinguish between the correct and the erroneous, and to resolve what is right and what is wrong—this is the meaning of "Southern."
There is a land named Supreme Bliss; because one awakens from this and brings these ten knowledges to perfect clarity, thereby shattering the darkness of the long night, it is called Supreme Bliss.
In that land there is a mountain named Wonderful Peak (Sumeru). For one who wishes to enter the stage of right determination, it shall not open unless they have attained meditative concentration.
To enter into supreme wisdom, one must take right stillness as the beginning.
"Mountain" signifies stillness; when the mind simply rests unmoving like a mountain, the objects of the mind are naturally seen through to their exhaustion.
When the mind ceases and appearances are exhausted, right wisdom immediately arises.

The exhaustion of marks arises from meditative concentration; wisdom is produced from concentration. Once concentration and wisdom are manifest, the delusions that constitute grasping and obstruction perish.
When the karma of grasping and the delusions have perished, great wisdom then appears.
When the marks are exhausted and their manifestation is fully known, it is called "Wondrous Peak.
By ascending to the summit of the mountain, one reaches the place where the marks are exhausted.

Within the principle of emptiness and signlessness, the wisdom of emptiness is perpetually luminous; the dust of karma from beginningless time is exhausted in a single thought-moment, such that body and mind are entirely exhausted and both internal and external are utterly obliterated.

When the five views—namely, the view of a self-identity, the grasping at views, the grasping at precepts and rituals, and wrong views—have been exhausted, this is called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Having seen the Path, the wisdom of emptiness alone constantly shines forth before one; one counteracts the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that follow one's conduct by means of this Path. As these habits are gradually thinned, wisdom becomes increasingly clear and luminous.

Once wisdom has increased, one extensively practices compassionate vows to deliver sentient beings; one shall pass away only when my vows are fulfilled, for as long as sentient beings are not exhausted, my practice shall not cease.

Great kindness is like the sun, universally illuminating the ten directions; great compassion is like the moon, bringing coolness to the ocean of existence. To remain thus from beginning to end without ceasing is called the cultivation of the Way.

Furthermore, for instance, Mount Wonderful Peak represents the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Here, the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance (*mūla-samantaprabhā-jñāna*) constitutes the essence of the path. By means of Mañjuśrī’s wondrous wisdom, one cultivates the practices of Samantabhadra to accomplish the path of Samantabhadra, acting as a gate of great compassion for the realm of sentient beings. One establishes the characteristics of the five stages, harmonizing and balancing the increase and decrease of wisdom and compassion until the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), at which point the process concludes and the ocean of wisdom is made increasingly luminous.

Great compassion is profound and vast; he is thoroughly proficient in all arts; his practice of the four means of integration is perfected; and his merit of loving-kindness and compassion is fulfilled, as detailed below in their proper sequence.
Thus, having completed the cultivation and purification from beginning to end, it does not transcend the realm of a single kṣaṇa. Seal this with wisdom; do not form conceptual attachments.

Thus, in this initial stage of the Bodhisattva Resolve, one clearly attains the gateway of fundamental wisdom through emptiness by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Ignorance begins to subside and wisdom begins to become clear; having been born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, it is called "abiding where the Buddhas abide. Therefore, one attains the Dharma-gate of the Universal Vision of the Wisdom-Light of the Realms of All Buddhas through Recollection.

By means of this path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is free from views of past and present, center and periphery, and so forth; traversing the five stages (*pañcāvasthā*) to refine habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and increase compassion is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Therefore, it is said that "at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening," for only then can one cultivate the path.
If the practices of higher wisdom and various arts are not perfected, they obstruct the bodhisattva conduct; thus, Sudhana traveled southward to seek out eminent spiritual friends, all of whom said:
"I have already previously generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; how should I learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?"

It is not said that the Buddha-way is increased; therefore, it is taken as fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) which is manifested through meditative concentration (samādhi). Being without action and without cultivation, one merely cultivates the bodhisattva path and studies the bodhisattva practices; fundamental wisdom then becomes self-evident and self-manifest, without any deliberate cultivation or effort.

Just as fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) constantly functions in conjunction with the practices of all Bodhisattvas—being unattached and unstained, and possessing a nature free from arising and ceasing, and free from birth and death—if one does not attain the essence of perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent; they all belong to the realms of humans and devas, subject to the karmic retribution of birth and death.
Regarding Sudhana’s seven days on Mount Supratiṣṭha: he is exhorted by the seven factors of enlightenment, hence the mention of "seven days.

His seeking and yearning in the four intermediate directions, above, and below refers to his practice of the ten-directional contemplation following meditative concentration, wherein he observes the essential nature of all phenomena.
From afar, he saw the bhikṣu Dechen walking slowly along a path on a separate mountain peak.
Because the mountain upon which he himself dwelt was his own basis for śamatha and vipaśyanā,
he saw this from afar with faith as being subsequent to śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Faith possesses the dharma-gate of the non-duality of stillness and function within meditative concentration and wisdom; for this reason, he walks slowly in circumambulation upon the mountain.

The mountain represents stillness (*samādhi*), while the slow walking in circumambulation represents function (*prajñā*). Because function exists without departing from stillness, it clarifies that one dwells neither in quiescence nor in agitation; therefore, he walks slowly in circumambulation.
"Having seen [him] and approaching" refers to ascending and progressing.
"Having arrived and joining the palms" signifies attaining accord with the truth.
"Prostrating" refers to reaching the fruit of one's original station.
"To circumambulate to the right" means to follow with faith and practice accordingly.

To proceed from the east to the north, from the west to the south, or from the north to the east constitutes circumambulation to the right; this follows the movement of the sun and does not depend on the lunar mansions. Now, those who practice the Way act contrary to this.
The Bhikṣu Meghābha said:

"I have attained the power of definitive understanding; my faculty of faith is pure, the light of wisdom shines radiantly, and as I universally contemplate all realms, I am free from all obstructions."
"Skillfully observing with a universally clear vision and possessing pure conduct;

proceeding to all lands in the ten directions to reverently make offerings to all Buddhas; constantly recollecting the *dhāraṇīs* of all Buddhas and the true Dharma of all Buddhas; constantly seeing all Buddhas of the ten directions—seeing one Buddha, two Buddhas, ten Buddhas, a hundred Buddhas, and even as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields"—this refers to the contemplation subsequent to the realization of the Path (*darśana-mārga*).
One should observe this with the Dharma-eye and the Wisdom-eye as before.
Having attained the power of resolute faith and understanding, my eye of faith is purified; that which is illuminated by the light of wisdom is precisely this.

With the light of the wisdom of the pure eye, they illuminate one Buddha, two Buddhas, a hundred Buddhas, a hundred thousand Buddhas, a billion Buddhas, ten billion Buddhas, a hundred billion Buddhas, nayuta-billions of Buddhas in the eastern direction, and even see countless, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, uncountable, inconceivable, unfathomable, unspeakable, and beyond-speakable Buddhas, even as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably-unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
This is the gateway of contemplation for entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the Buddha’s realm, making offerings to all Buddhas, and training in the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva.

In response to what was previously requested by Sudhana—namely, how to swiftly bring the practices of Samantabhadra to full completion—the practitioner should, with the eye of the light of pure wisdom, rely solely upon this Dharma and observe from the eastern direction that the minds of all sentient beings are like one's own mind: they are without substance, without characteristics, and without the nature of mind; one does not perceive any marks of sentient beings such as suffering or pleasure, good or evil, right or wrong, long or short.

Relying solely on the eye of pure wisdom, its radiance shines universally, perceiving only the true essence of all sentient beings, rather than following what is seen by the physical eyes of emotional consciousness.
One perceives only the essence of the fruits of merit of all sentient beings, appearing as the marks of the Buddhas, and does not perceive the marks of humans, devas, the evil realms, or the hells.
All objective realms are like light and like shadows—neither real nor unreal—their nature being inherently stainless.
All Buddhas, sentient beings, and one's own self are, in their fundamental essence and characteristics, originally of a single flavor.
One must give rise to the ocean-like realm of the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*), all of which is produced through wisdom.

The realm of the signless Dharmakāya is such that the essence of wisdom is fundamentally non-existent and all phenomena are empty and quiescent; it is like Maitreya’s pavilion, which comes from nowhere and, upon its cessation, goes nowhere.

To see the entire realm of all sentient beings as the realm of nirvāṇa, and to see the entire realm of sentient beings as the realm of the Tathāgata, does not arise from what is known through deluded sentiments, but follows the illumination of the light of wisdom. This renders existence and non-existence sovereign, such that one sees all sentient beings without impairing the fleshly eye;
sees that realms have no inherent substance without impairing the Dharma-eye;
and sees the bodies of all Buddhas as manifesting myriad realms through illusion with total mastery without impairing the wisdom-eye.

The Dharma-gate of the Miraculous Transformation of the Great Functioning Radiance of Non-constructive Wisdom is entirely produced by illusory wisdom; it has no existence either internally or externally.

From the east and the four intermediate directions, extending upward and downward to infinity, one brings about mastery through the functioning of the radiance of pure wisdom. One must first manifest the signless, universal radiance of pure wisdom through the meditative concentration of non-constructive self-nature, and only when free from the karma of greed and hatred and endowed with a heart of compassion can one enter this Dharma-gate of the illusion of wisdom where existence and non-existence are both mastered.

If one does not possess the karma of compassion, one will become a powerful ghost or spirit, a malevolent yakṣa, or a malevolent rākṣasa, as described in the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra."
This is the contemplation following the Path of Vision; those who have not yet entered the realm of wisdom are not yet capable of it.

If one exclusively contemplates emptiness and purifies karma, the mind becomes attached to the principle of emptiness and its subtle functions fail to operate; this results in stagnation in quiescence, which is the seed of the practice of the Two Vehicles.

If one is deluded regarding the wondrous spirit of principle and wisdom, and exclusively engages in contemplation with the notion of conditioned activity, this is simply the realm of conditioned arising and ceasing, identical to the visualization of Amitābha’s Pure Land in the West.

This contemplative gateway of the wisdom-realm of the One Vehicle causes the wondrous light of pure, non-active wisdom to become a gateway of great function, arising from the pure, great wisdom-light of the fundamental, signless Dharmakāya; therein one studies the spiritual powers of the Bodhisattvas and enters the path of Samantabhadra.

Those who maintain a one-sided conceptualization will not arrive at the goal; those whose minds are predominantly fixed on absolute truth alone will also fail to achieve it. Only when one turns from the absolute toward its functional application can the practice be undertaken.
As in the sutra, the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī praised what Sudhana sought:

"You seek the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva, even seeking the gates of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa for a bodhisattva, and you seek the bodhisattva’s observation of the conditioned and the unconditioned with a mind free from attachment."

Therefore, this Dharma-gate that opens the entrance to the Buddha’s realm is taught; it is the Dharma-gate that harmonizes birth-and-death with nirvana, and the conditioned with the unconditioned, while remaining free from attachment.
By means of the light of pure great wisdom, one enters the great function of a bodhisattva, for its wondrous application of supernatural powers is eternally quiescent.

He paced slowly in walking meditation upon the summit of a separate mountain, manifesting that movement and stillness have found their proper place; for this reason, his body did not remain seated even while sitting.

Having entered the Path of Seeing through practice, he contemplated with the light of right wisdom in this manner, following the sūtras as a gateway to essence and function, ensuring there was no partial study to obstruct his progress.
By accomplishing a single gate of contemplation in this life, one shall immediately upon rebirth enter the great function of the divine power of retributive karma with sovereign ease.
This occurs within a single kṣaṇa; it can be seen by illuminating it with perfect wisdom in the next life.
For example, in the visualization of the Western Pure Land, one exclusively forms conceptualizations of conditioned phenomena;
yet, because these are accomplished through the power of mental intention, one still attains the supernormal powers of the karma of transformational birth and death.

If even those who perform the ten wholesome karmas are reborn in the heavens and obtain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as a result of their karma—such as dragons and powerful spirits—then it follows that even those with the evil karma of ignorance still possess supernormal powers.

How much more so for one whose Dharma-eye has blossomed, who employs the power of the roots of goodness of kindness and compassion to direct the faculties of wisdom, and who applies their attention for a single lifetime—how could such a person fail to attain great utility and supernormal powers in a future life?

To clarify that the initial arousal of the mind constitutes the attainment of perfect enlightenment: this refers to the fundamental, universal light-wisdom (samantaprabhā-jñāna) of the signless Dharma-body.

Taking the principle of non-action as the essence of perfect enlightenment, one achieves spiritual powers (abhijñā) through this; such is the bodhisattva practice of the essence of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.

Now, at the time when the aspiration for enlightenment is generated in this present life, one attains right wisdom and accomplishes the mind through contemplative practice upon the body of segmented existence, while concurrently cultivating wholesome virtues and various arts.

When the mind is perfected through contemplative practice, one enters the body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*) in a future life. This is because the present body of segmented existence (*pariccheda-kāya*) is the result of past karma; by cultivating the practice of contemplation with wisdom in this life, one attains birth through divine power and transformation in the next life.
That which is attained only after each individual has perfected their own practice is it.
That which is attained through the power of one's own practice is the true.
That which is attained through the temporary power of the Buddha’s or Bodhisattvas’ empowerment is not true; once that divine power is withdrawn, one returns to one's former state.

Just as when one is under the empowering influence of spirits or ghosts, it constitutes a demonic activity; the person's mind is transformed so that they lack self-mastery, and their mind immediately becomes deranged and unrecoverable.

Each and every one, by the power of their own realization of the Path, clearly perceives that the mind and its objects are devoid of substantiality; they purify the karma of greed, hatred, and delusion through the inherently pure and impartial nature of great compassionate activity, which is of one essence with all beings. Thus, they see without seeing and know without knowing, so that all their actions are truly authentic.

Taking wisdom as its function, it employs the seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*) to seal the karmic fruits of the three periods of time for all sentient beings; this constitutes, in total, the realm of the Buddha, whereby one’s own mind finally attains freedom from defilement.

From the passage "Since I have attained this Dharma-gate of the Universal Vision of the Wisdom-Light of All Buddhas through Recollection" onwards, this constitutes the advancement by means of attributing virtue.

This preceding section marks the initial entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; here, wisdom universally encompasses the realms of all Buddhas of the three periods of time as a single moment. Within the one true Dharma-realm, there is no nature of past or present; thus, one perceives neither newly enlightened Buddhas nor long-established Buddhas. Because the Dharma possesses no nature of past or present, new or old, formation or destruction, it is perceived with the universal eye.
The second stage, the Dwelling of Purifying the Ground, takes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) as its primary focus, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.
Regarding the meaning of the south, it is explained as before.
As for the land in the south named the Land of the Sea Gate (*Samudra-mukha*), it takes the perfection of ethical discipline as the essence of that sea gate.

Because the great ocean does not harbor corpses, it takes the light of wisdom of the Dharma-body as its essence of precepts; being pure by nature, it does not harbor the corpses of afflictions, evil karma, the seeds of consciousness, various views, greed, and hatred.
Taking the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance of the Dharma-body as the essence of the precepts, for its nature is inherently stainless.

When this wisdom manifests, the ocean of birth and death consisting of the twelve links of existence becomes the great ocean of merit, the ocean of virtue, and the ocean of eloquence of all Buddhas; therefore, it is called the "Gate of the Ocean."
As the sūtra itself states:
"The bhikṣu Sāgaramegha" represents the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), which constitute the great ocean of afflictions and karma of all sentient beings.

Now, through the purity of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, one becomes the great ocean of all Buddhas—the ocean of universal radiance wisdom, the ocean of all merits, and the ocean of great wisdom—able to manifest this Dharma to provide shelter, moisture, and benefit for all sentient beings, causing them to awaken; thus, the twelve links of existence become an ocean of clouds.
Therefore, Sudhana went to the place of the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, prostrated at his feet, thereby clarifying his advancement to this stage.
He joined his palms, thereby clarifying his harmonious realization of the dharma of this stage.
Sudhana said,
"Having first resolved my mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I wish to enter the ocean of all unsurpassed wisdom.
This clarifies Sudhana’s request for the Dharma, as explained at length in the sutra.

The bhikṣu Sāgaramegha praised Sudhana for being able to resolve upon bodhicitta, stating that he must attain the light of the roots of goodness of the Universal Door, possess the light of wisdom from the samādhi of the true path, generate various great merits, and increase pure dharmas; furthermore, he must serve spiritual friends without weariness or rest, never giving rise to fatigue or aversion, disregarding his own body and life, and possessing no hoarded stores.
As explained at length in the sutra, the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha said:

"I have lived for twelve years in the country of Sāgaramukha, constantly taking the great ocean as my sphere of activity; that is to say, I contemplate the immeasurable jewels and marvelous adornments of the great ocean."
The details are as explained in the sutra.
As for the statement "dwelling in the kingdom of Samudramukha for twelve years," it means dwelling in the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
By contemplating the ocean of birth and death through the twelve links of dependent origination, one thereby becomes a great ocean of wisdom.
Extending even to the wondrous adornments of immeasurable various jewels, [the text] clarifies the delusions regarding the twelve links of dependent origination:

ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, sickness, death, and suffering.
Sighing and lamenting, weeping with grief and sorrow, they are followed by the fruits of suffering without respite.

Now, through the power of the skillful means of Samādhi-contemplation, this becomes a pure ocean of great luminous wisdom, an ocean of all merits, an ocean of exquisite adornments of every kind of jewel, and an ocean of immeasurable wisdom.
As explained extensively in the sūtras,

delusion regarding these twelve links of existence results in immeasurable fruits of suffering, adorned by the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and the miseries of poverty and affliction.
If one employs the power of skillful means through the observation of meditative concentration and wisdom, one then becomes an ocean of all Buddhas and an ocean of all merits and wisdom.

Just as the twelve links of existence arise solely from delusion regarding three factors: first, failing to realize that the essence of mind and objects is empty, and instead directly grasping at mind and objects as truly existent, is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
The second [delusion] takes name-and-form as its object.

The third takes the six sense faculties as primary; because the mental faculty (manas) does not understand, it becomes deluded regarding name-and-form. Through the mutual correspondence of faculty and object, volitional formations (saṃskāra), contact (sparśa), sensation (vedanā), craving (tṛṣṇā), grasping (upādāna), and becoming (bhava) give rise to the karma that produces consciousness.
Due to these three conditions, the twelve links of dependent origination continue in succession, and the fruits of suffering within the three realms never cease.
Now, by applying the power of skillful means, one treats this condition to bring about the work of great wisdom and cut off the flowing stream of birth and death.

By means of meditative concentration, one stills one's own mental faculty (*manas*), so that within the five sense faculties, it does not take objects as its conditions and the mental faculty does not arise; consequently, the other five faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—do not arise either.

Once the faculty of mind is purified, both the mind and its objects vanish; there is neither internal nor external, neither great nor small, and no distinction between the three periods of time or past and present—the seeds of discriminative consciousness are entirely extinguished.

With the cessation of the mind, the twelve links of dependent origination cease; the entire fruit of suffering within the three realms ceases, leaving only true wisdom—luminous, clear, and brilliantly illuminating the ten directions.
Wisdom and its objects—the myriad phenomena—lack inherent substance. Because wisdom lacks substance and is fundamentally luminous and pure, its measure is equal to empty space.
Being coextensive with the dharma-realm and devoid of center or periphery, its divine function is omnipresent, for it has neither coming nor going.
One enters the realms of all multitudes as being like a flame, a transformation, an illusion, a shadow, or space, because there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
Wisdom itself is selfless, for it perceives no other master.
Wisdom is inherently non-reliant, for it does not perceive anything else upon which to depend and abide.
Wisdom is identical to the Dharma-realm, for all that is perceived is the Dharma.
Wisdom is identical to pure and wondrous radiance, for it manifests all objective forms while universally encompassing them.
Wisdom is the sublime spirit, for it is devoid of intrinsic nature and is skillfully able to discern the affairs of the ten directions.
Wisdom is pure like space; it evokes the arising of an ocean of merit, for all are equally like the wondrous adornments of light and shadow.

Wisdom is like Indra’s net; it universally manifests its body before all objects and all sentient beings, appearing as physical forms according to the distinctions of their karma, for it is devoid of coming or going.
Wisdom is like the water-purifying jewel; when it manifests in a single thought-moment, the turbid waters of beginningless ignorance and the twelve links of existence are purified all at once.

Therefore, when ignorance ceases, the ocean of suffering of birth and death—the twelve links of existence consisting of roots, objects, and consciousness—ceases simultaneously. The self-nature of the *dharmadhātu*, the universally radiant wisdom, and the ocean of all merit and wisdom manifest and open forth all at once.

Therefore, by encouraging the contemplation of the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and the six sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses, one accomplishes the ocean of all merits of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; thereby one attains the light of the wisdom of all Buddhas, wherein all phenomena on Mount Sumeru are exhausted, and the function of the supramundane path becomes lofty and manifest.

"Contemplate the twelve links of existence—the seeds of the six sense faculties, name-and-form, and consciousness—as they manifest, so that you may penetrate the world and accomplish all the merits that constitute the seed of omniscience.
The bhikṣu Sāgaramegha said: "Noble son!"
"When I was thinking this thought, a great lotus suddenly appeared from beneath this great ocean.
Its stem is made of the Indrāṇī Jewel 'Invincible,' and it is named after the Lord of Devas, for he is the sovereign among all jewels."

Nīla is a pure and exquisite blue jewel; it symbolizes that which arises from the practice of the dāna-pāramitā produced as the retributive fruit of fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), while the remaining nine pāramitās are assigned to it in successive order.

The hundred thousand asura kings who hold the stalks of lotuses represent the myriad practices performed by Bodhisattvas; these are attained without departing from the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance, for they dwell within birth and death with mastery rather than being submerged. This is like the asuras dwelling in the great ocean without being drowned.

Regarding the hundred thousand dragon kings raining down fragrant water: taking the wisdom of mastery over distinctions as the essence of the precepts—this wisdom is like a dragon, constantly dwelling in the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā), raining down the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, which serves as the fragrant water.

Because the essence of wisdom is eternally empty, pure and stainless, and capable of purifying all karmic actions, it is taken as the essence of the precepts; thus it is likened to a dragon, which soars through the void and brings down rain.
The remaining [features] are assigned according to the practice of the *pāramitās*.
These other various jewel adornments are born as the retribution for the practice of the ten *pāramitās*, and this lotus possesses such adornments.

"The fragrance spreads, pervades, protects, and covers the great ocean" means that while the intrinsic nature of the myriad practices is untainted, they are able to universally shelter all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm; this is symbolized by the lotus flower.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "This great lotus flower arises from the roots of goodness of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world; it manifests before all worlds in the ten directions.

It is born from dharmas that are like illusions, born from dharmas that are like dreams, and born from pure karma. It is adorned by the dharma-gate of non-contention, enters the seal of the unconditioned, abides in the gate of non-obstruction, and fills all lands throughout the ten directions."
Upon a lotus flower there is a Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture.
As for his body extending from here up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) constitutes the essence of the Buddha.

Since the essence of wisdom is fundamentally non-existent, its divine function is wondrously pure and exhausts the ocean of all existence; it is perfected throughout the ten directions, such that no limit can be seen.
Regarding the statement "extending upward to the Peak of Existence," this refers to the ultimate limit of all forms and objects perceived within the realms of existence.
As the Sūtra says, "The mark of the invisible crown of the head is inconceivable.

When it is said that the Tathāgata extends his right hand to stroke my head, the right hand represents the method of active function, while stroking the head signifies the guidance toward and realization of the True.
The Way is harmonized and certified because doubts have been removed.
When you say, "Speak the Puyan Sūtra for me," it is to clarify our mutual accord.
The eye of wisdom is universally pervasive, its measure equal to the Dharma-realm.
Observing universally the faculties and their objects, teachings arise in accordance with the faculties; as faculties and objects are infinite, teachings are likewise inexhaustible.
If there were no faculties and objects, teachings would fundamentally cease to exist.

This clarifies that fundamental wisdom establishes teachings in response to phenomena; because it treats all sentient beings with equality and its capacity pervades all roots, it is called the *Puyan Jing* (Universal Eye Sutra).

The sutra states: "Suppose there were a person who took the waters of the great ocean for ink and the mass of Mount Sumeru for a brush to transcribe this Universal Eye Dharma-gate—writing a single gate within a single chapter, a single dharma within a single gate, a single meaning within a single dharma, and a single phrase within a single meaning—they could not grasp even a small fraction of it, let alone be able to complete it all."

Since the teaching does not arise of itself but originates from the interaction of the faculties and their objects, and since sentient beings are infinite while their fetters of affliction are manifold, these faculties and objects are boundless and the gates of teaching are inexhaustible. Thus, fundamental wisdom serves as the Universal Eye, and discriminative wisdom constitutes the Sūtras.

For twelve hundred years in the presence of that Buddha, I upheld this Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye. Day by day, through the light of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, I received countless chapters; these represent the fact that the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination possesses one hundred afflictions. From the ten types of ignorance, their mutual essences number one hundred, as they pervade the twelve links. Within the twelve links, there are ten conditions for each link, resulting in one thousand two hundred roots of great affliction. These act as immeasurable conditions for delusion for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, causing them to wander in the great ocean of birth and death.

Now, by means of the power of skillful means observed through meditative concentration, one becomes a sea of pure, universal radiance wisdom and a sea of differentiated wisdom; for this reason, it is called "upholding such a Universal Eye Sutra for twelve hundred years."

By means of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), one gives rise from fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*) to immeasurable Dharma-gates for benefiting sentient beings; this is what is meant by "I, in the presence of that Buddha, received and upheld [them].

This clarifies that through the wisdom that completely transcends the entanglements—manifesting as the characteristics of Mount Sumeru—one practices the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination to remedy the ocean of suffering of birth and death within the six sense bases, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and consciousness. Thus, one accomplishes the Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye of Pure Wisdom-Light, causing the ocean of birth and death to become an ocean of wisdom and compassion.
From the passage "Since I have known only this Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye" onwards, this is the section on advancing by inferring [the Buddha's] virtues.
Thus, these eighty-four thousand afflictions all arise without departing from the five aggregates and the six sense faculties—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

It is merely name-and-form and the six sense organs; because the mental faculty (manas) does not fully comprehend the objects of name-and-form among the five [physical] faculties, there arise the twelve links of dependent origination and the ten great afflictions, which constitute the eighty-four thousand [afflictions].
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Within each of the five aggregates, there are one hundred afflictions; thus, across the five aggregates, there are five hundred afflictions."
"There are five hundred within and five hundred without; thus it continues up to eighty-four thousand.
This clarifies that upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), there are one thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) categorized as internal and external.
Regarding the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there are one thousand for each single tendency, totaling ten thousand across the ten.
Furthermore, when these ten underlying tendencies are divided into internal and external categories, there are ten thousand in each, making twenty thousand in total.

Due to the predominance of greed, hatred, and delusion, there are sixty-three thousand [types of individuals]: totaling twenty-one thousand who predominantly exhibit greedy behavior, twenty-one thousand who predominantly exhibit hateful behavior, and twenty-one thousand who predominantly exhibit deluded behavior.
The three categories, each numbering twenty-one thousand, constitute eighty-four thousand.

Four thousand is the fundamental count of the internal and external aspects of the five aggregates; eighty thousand is the count of the instances of greed, hatred, and delusion arising from the objects of the ten proclivities. All these, through the three factors of the six sense organs, name-and-form, and consciousness, give rise to inexhaustible afflictions that constitute the great delusion pervading the realms of the ten directions.
Among these three matters, the mind-faculty (*manas*) is primary.

Now, it is simply because the pure intention of meditative concentration realizes that [the self] was originally non-existent, and the five [sense-faculties] were fundamentally without a master, that all internal and external realms—the mountains, rivers, great earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth—are all grasped as signs by the mind-faculty, giving rise to consciousness and forming attachments; this is termed the seven consciousnesses.
It is merely given a name based on the locus of its grasping, yet it has no separate substance.

Following the locus where karma is formed, it arises within the tainted realms of the three worlds and is termed the eighth seed; it too has no separate substance, but is simply that which is constituted by a single manovijñāna.

Now, when the practitioner simply brings the faculty of mind to rest, unmoving like a mountain, the mind and its objects naturally exhaust one another; the mind perishes and objects fade away, consciousness ceases, and wisdom is perfected.

The delusions of the dust of beginningless time arise solely from the confusion of the mind; when the mind perishes, wisdom manifests, and the ten directions become luminous and clear, while the mind and its objects are empty and void—this is called the Ground of Wisdom.

With the sun of wisdom, one universally observes that the myriad phenomena have no essence or characteristics; they are born from the illusory emptiness of delusion, having neither beginning nor end, and lacking any substance of birth and death. The three realms, the six paths of humans, devas, asuras, earth, and hells—all worlds without exception—are produced solely by the false dust of mental conceptions.
Because the mind ceases, delusory objects accordingly cease, just as fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
When the mind is spent, karma becomes empty; the four great elements likewise pass away, and the mountains, rivers, and the great earth perish along with the mind.

This is not a state of dissipation where emotions have vanished and thoughts are entirely exhausted; it is known only through correspondence with right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), and does not depend on the deliberations of emotional consciousness.

The Master’s verse says: "The mountains, rivers, the great earth, and fire and wind— The realms of the three worlds arise from the mind. When the mental consciousness is extinguished like empty space, All realms are simultaneously extinguished."

When the consciousness of mental objects ceases, delusive realms vanish; there remains only the wondrous adornment of the realm of true wisdom. This adornment of the realm of wisdom is like light and shadow—mutually illuminating and penetrating, neither existent nor non-existent.
The realm of wisdom is bodiless and without vision; because wisdom is pure, its activity is thus.
With great wisdom illuminating the world, one does not see the world, but only the realm of wisdom.
"One is able to see the world with the fleshly eye,
yet remains free from attachment toward what is seen. He asked:

Since the fundamental wisdom is inherently stainless in its own essence, why is it not naturally and originally the Buddha? For what reason can it follow delusion to become the sentient beings of the six realms, wandering in the ocean of suffering?
If that which is attained through cultivation were subject to arising and ceasing and impermanent, it would belong to the causes and effects of humans and devas;

if it were not attained through cultivation, why would one not naturally be a Buddha, yet instead becomes a sentient being, experiencing suffering and joy, with the distinctions of birth and death within the six realms?
The answer is:
Because for that true wisdom, there is no self-nature and no fundamental essence; it is immutably and eternally abiding. To say "I am the Buddha" is because it is intrinsically pure by nature.
Because there is no intrinsic nature, there is no self-existent "I" who is a Buddha or who is pure.

If there were a self-existent "I" who is a Buddha, who is pure, who is wisdom, or who has attained perfect enlightenment, then there would be a locus and a dharma that could be apprehended; this would be the view of eternalism and it would be a form of nihilism.

If one observes carefully the ten directions, not a single such thing exists; there is only that which is eternally quiescent. If such things did exist, there would not be the ten directions and the three realms with their suffering and joy, long lives and short lives, the diversity of all phenomena, or the distinctions among sentient beings.

If there were no intrinsic nature that remained eternally and immutably constant, it would necessarily depend upon conditions to be manifested; it is not something produced through cultivation or effort. Because wisdom lacks intrinsic nature, it does not belong to that which is eternally and immutably constant, nor does it belong to that which is produced through cultivation or effort; both of these two categories fall under the views of annihilationism and eternalism.

Because there is no intrinsic nature, the deluded mind and its objects give rise to attachment; this forms the causes of karma and the grasping at lightness or heaviness. With many emotional reactions of aversion or compliance—such as hatred, love, greed, and ignorance—there arise the various sufferings and pleasures of birth and death within the six realms of existence.
Due to the afflictions of grasping at karma, aversion, desire, and attachment, various types of karma arise.

From among these lighter afflictions, for those who possess the fruits of human and celestial happiness, it is only by knowing the suffering of birth and death that they can attain the noble wisdom of self-awakening.

There are those who resolve their minds [for enlightenment] because of a teacher; they all do so because they realize that birth and death are long and far-reaching, and only then do they set their will upon seeking the True Path.
None of them become Buddhas spontaneously or by natural birth.
This is true wisdom because it is devoid of self-nature (*svabhāva*).

Even among devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, only those who can perceive the faults of the long-term cycle of birth and death, or who take the prior wisdom of the sages as their teacher to achieve awakening and purify the state of mind, are able to manifest that the fundamental mind is without nature. Only then do they realize that all objects of mental perception are entirely without nature; that both self-nature and the states of mind are unarisen—this is called the realm of wisdom.
Because it manifests through wisdom, one then illuminates that all objects to which the mind is deluded are entirely non-existent; this is what is called the "sphere of wisdom.

Now, the causes and effects of the triple world are all obtained through the operation of karma, whereas wisdom is manifested through the concentration of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Only then can one realize that wisdom itself has no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); it neither creates ignorance nor brings about Buddhahood, because wisdom itself has no intrinsic nature and because one realizes that everything is entirely without intrinsic nature.
Ignorance does not arise because wisdom is inherently devoid of self-nature; nor does it arise because there is a Buddha who is eternally present by nature.
Therefore, the teachings state:
"All phenomena do not arise from themselves, for they depend upon conditions."
It does not arise from another, because all conditions are themselves devoid of intrinsic nature.

It does not arise from both [self and other], because wisdom and the essence of practice are empty and lack intrinsic nature, and thus possess neither the nature of conjunction nor the nature of separation.
"It does not arise without cause; it is only through awakening and cultivation that it becomes manifest, for it is not spontaneously accomplished.

It is accomplished without being accomplished and destroyed without being destroyed, because wisdom that is without dependence neither accomplishes itself nor destroys itself; this is because such wisdom does not belong to accomplishment or destruction, and does not belong to annihilation or permanence.
Because one awakens through wisdom to the absence of intrinsic nature, one does not belong to birth and death.
Because one awakens through wisdom to the fact that there is no place of dependence for oneself, one does not belong to birth and death.
Because one awakens through wisdom to the fact that there is no place of dependence for oneself, one does not belong to any obtainable location.

The Spirit employs the ten directions, manifesting itself in accordance with the faculties of beings; it is not swift yet reaches everywhere. Within the Spirit there is no Spirit, yet it can exercise great function; within Wisdom there is no Wisdom, yet it can achieve great illumination. In sum, it is formless and without substance, being entirely empty.
Because it is void and non-existent, water and fire cannot cause calamity, sharp blades cannot inflict injury, and birth and death cannot bring about change.

Though spoken of as empty, it possesses the great spiritual function of the Great Emptiness; though spoken of as existent, no form or characteristic can be apprehended. It is vast yet does not expand, minute yet does not contract. These names are illusorily produced for the benefit of those who have not yet attained clarity, for within these names there is no name.

That which is known is like an echo; seeing the essence of all Tathāgatas is like light and shadow; teaching and transforming sentient beings is like a mirage; giving rise to great vows is like the wind; practicing compassion is like clouds raining down; and through the wisdom of space, one encompasses all phenomena, sharing their same substance without ever wearying of them or abandoning them.
To all sentient beings, he manifests his form-body, pervading everywhere in a single thought-moment, yet without an agent.
